part.reserve.title: Spare tempo
part.reserve.summary: A pawn advance that does not harm the position passes the turn without moving the kings: with it, the opposition changes hands.
ex.e14: Play as White and find the best move. All the pawns are blocked, on the a and g files. Your king is on e3 and the black king is on d7. Whoever has to move first gives up ground.
ex.e14.hint: The white king must lose a tempo without approaching the black king at once. If it advances right away, Black draws.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd3! is the waiting move: the king loses a tempo, and now Black has to move. 1.Ke4? and 1.Kd4? bring the king up too early and only draw. After 1...Kd6, 2.Kd4! takes the direct opposition; after 2...Ke6, 3.Ke4! repeats the opposition with Black to move. With no pawn moves, Black keeps giving up ground, and the white king enters on the chosen wing.
ex.e15: Play as White and find the best move. The b-file pawns are blocked, each king protects its own, and both sides still have pawn moves on the f-file.
ex.e15.hint: The king that has to move first abandons its pawn. Think about how to spend the f-file pawn moves so that the turn is left to Black.
ex.e15.solution: 1.f4! closes the gap between the f-file pawns: no pawn can move any more, and Black has to play with the king. After 1...Kd4, 2.Kxb5! captures the pawn, and your b-pawn promotes. 1.f3? leaves one empty square and loses the fight: 1...f4! and it is your king that has to move; after 2.Ka6 Kxb4 Black is a pawn up and wins. 1.Ka6? or 1.Kb6? also lose: 1...Kxb4 captures the pawn, and 1...f4 wins as well. On the second turn only the capture wins: 2.Ka6? Ke3 and the black king captures on f4, with a draw.
ex.e16: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is close to your g3 pawn, your king is on the edge, and the b-file pawns are not yet touching.
ex.e16.hint: Think about the pawn moves each side still keeps on the b-file, and do not let the black king reach the g3 pawn without your king nearby.
ex.e16.solution: 1.b4! fixes the b5 pawn before the king acts: Black is left without a reserve move on the b-file. 1.Kg7? b4! and it is Black who keeps the last tempo; after 2.Kf6 Kg4 3.Kg6 Kxg3 the black g-pawn promotes, and your king does not get back in time. After 1...g4, only 2.Kg7! holds: 2.Kg8? Kg6! and the black king reaches f3 via f5 and e4. After 2...Kg5, 3.Kh7! waits: 3.Kf7? Kf5! 4.Ke7 Ke4 5.Kd6 Kf3 and the g3 pawn falls with no compensation. After 3...Kf5, 4.Kh6! goes after the g4 pawn: 4...Ke4 5.Kg5 Kd3 6.Kxg4 Kc3 7.Kf3 Kxb4 and each king has captured a pawn. The two remaining pawns both promote: a draw.
part.waiting.title: Waiting with kings
part.waiting.summary: If bringing the king closer stalemates the opponent, wait with the king; spend your pawn move only after he has spent his.
part.fixedTarget.title: Fix first
part.fixedTarget.summary: First blockade the pawn that would give the opponent a spare move: without it, the turn does not change, and your king reaches the defence in time.
part.secondReserve.title: Save a tempo
part.secondReserve.summary: A pawn on the second rank gives two waiting moves if it advances one square at a time; save the second for when the king needs to change the turn.
ex.e14.r1: The black king goes to d6, facing your king. The pawns are blocked: only the kings can wait.
ex.e14.r2: The black king goes to e6, trying to keep pace with the white king. Black has no pawn move.
ex.e15.r1: The black king goes to d4: the pawns no longer move, and it has to abandon the b5 pawn.
ex.e16.r1: The black pawn advances to g4 and fixes your g3 pawn; the black king will try to go around it to capture.
ex.e16.r2: The black king goes to g5 and tries to pass along the f-file, towards the g3 pawn.
ex.e16.r3: The black king goes to f5: it wants to reach e4 and f3 to capture the g3 pawn.
title: Waiting moves
summary: Changing the turn with a spare pawn move or a king waiting move, to keep the opposition and force the enemy king to give way.
history:
In many pawn endings what decides is not who has the closer king, but who is forced to move first. A pawn that can still advance without consequences is a spare tempo: it lets you pass the move to the opponent. A king move that changes nothing, made only to wait, is a waiting move. Whoever can count these moves turns a seemingly equal position into a win or a draw.

The Soviet master {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}} composed famous studies on the theme in the early twentieth century, in which two pawns and two kings seem frozen and yet only one precise waiting move keeps the result.
practice: Now the real ending: king on e1, pawn on f3, and the black king on c8. Bring the king in front of the pawn, toward the key squares e5, f5 and g5, and use the opposition to reach one of them. Pick your pace and go.
key.grigoriev: A study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, from 1933. Black keeps the advance of the d5 pawn in reserve, a move to change the turn whenever convenient. White needs waiting moves that still work after the reserve is spent.
ex.e20: Play as White and find the best move. The a-file pawns are fixed, and the black king escorts the h6 pawn. Your king is beside it.
ex.e20.hint: Your king cannot reach the a5 pawn in time. Find out how to stop the black king from advancing, following it move by move.
ex.e20.solution: 1.Kf5! stays beside the black king, on the same rank, with one square between them: lateral opposition. 1.Kg3? or 1.Kf3? Kg5! and the black king keeps the opposition: it escorts the h-pawn or goes for the a4 pawn. 1.Ke4? or 1.Ke5? Kg5! and the h-pawn advances with an escort. After 1...Kh4, 2.Kf4! follows; 2.Kg6? h5! 3.Kf5 Kg3 and the pawn gets through. After 2...h5, 3.Kf3! and the black king cannot advance: 3.Kf5? Kg3! and it slips behind your king. After 3...Kh3 4.Kf4 h4 5.Kf3 Kh2 6.Kf2 h3 7.Kf1 the h-pawn does not promote: a draw.
ex.e20.r1: The black king goes to h4 and tries to pass through g3.
ex.e20.r2: The black pawn advances to h5: Black tries to pass the turn to your king.
ex.e21: Play as White and find the best move. Each side still has one pawn move and the kings are close; the black king attacks your b4 pawn.
ex.e21.hint: The black king threatens your pawn. Once that is settled, hold the draw with the kings facing each other, always with one square between them.
ex.e21.solution: 1.b5! saves the pawn: it steps out of the black king's reach. After 1...b6, nobody has a pawn move left, and the draw comes from the opposition: 2.Kd2! and, after 2...Kc4, 3.Kc2! and, after 3...Kb4, 4.Kb2! Your king faces the black king, with one square between them, and it cannot get in. Beware of 2.Kd4? Kb4: the b5 pawn falls, and the b6 pawn promotes.
ex.e21.r1: The black pawn goes to b6 and fixes the structure: now only the kings move.
ex.e21.r2: The black king climbs to c4, trying to enter through the centre.
ex.e21.r3: The black king goes to b4, aiming at the b5 pawn.
ex.e22: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is on the edge, on h7, and each side has an a-file pawn. Find the move that takes the reserve away from Black.
ex.e22.hint: Whoever can still move the a-file pawn has a reserve move. Stop Black from using theirs when it needs it.
ex.e22.solution: 1.a5! advances the pawn and takes away the pawn move Black would use to pass the turn. 1.Kh5? a5! and it is Black who spends the reserve move at the right moment: your king has to move, and the h6 pawn does not promote: a draw. After 1.a5 Kh8, 2.Kg6 and the white king reaches the a6 pawn; the win is certain.
coach.allPartsDone: Now you know how to use a waiting move to hand the move back to your opponent. Shall we go to the final test?
ex.e17.hint: Whoever moves the king first loses the opposition. Count the pawn moves each side still keeps before deciding.
ex.e17.solution: 1.b5! is the spare tempo: the pawn passes the turn, the kings stay as they were, with the opposition for you, and the b6 pawn is fixed. Now the black king has to give way: after 1...Kc7, 2.Ke6 (or 2.Ke5) Kb7 3.Kd6 Ka8 4.Kc6 Ka7 5.Kc7 Ka8 6.Kxb6 and the b-pawn promotes. 1.Kc4? Kc6! and the black king keeps the opposition: a draw. 1.Ke5? b5! and it is Black who passes the turn: a draw.
ex.e17: Play as White and find the best move. The kings face each other on the d-file, with one square between them, and each side still has a pawn that can move.
ex.e23: Play as White and find the best move. The kings stand in front of the central pawns: your king defends the e5 pawn, and the black king defends the one on e6.
ex.e23.hint: If your king leaves, the e5 pawn falls. Whom do you want to force to move the king?
ex.e23.solution: 1.h4! is the spare tempo: the pawn passes the turn without moving the king, and Black is in zugzwang. The black king cannot keep defending e6: after 1...Ke4, 2.Kxe6 and the e5 pawn promotes with the king's help; after 1...Kg6, 2.Kxe6 just the same. A king move such as 1.Kd7? or 1.Kc5? abandons the e5 pawn: 1...Kxe5 and Black draws.
ex.e24: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is in the a8 corner, and the b6 pawn is close to promotion. Beware of stalemate: choose your king's square carefully.
ex.e24.hint: Coming too close takes away every square from the black king. Leave it one free square, and advance the pawn when the black king steps out of the corner.
ex.e24.solution: 1.Kc6! waits and leaves the black king the b8 square. 1.Kc7? is stalemate at once: the black king has no move, and the game is drawn. After 1...Kb8, 2.b7! advances with the black king out of the corner; after 2...Ka7, 3.Kc7! guards b8, and the pawn will promote. If 3.b8=Q+?, 3...Kxb8 captures the queen and draws.
ex.e24.r1: The black king leaves the corner by the only free square.
ex.e24.r2: The black king goes to a7, the only square it has left.
